analysis.one_liner: Makes meat contaminated with dangerous E. coli strains illegal to sell.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Agriculture Committee with zero cosponsors at the end of the 111th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change federal meat inspection law so that any meat contaminated with Shiga toxin-producing E. coli — the bacteria that cause severe food poisoning, kidney failure, and sometimes death — would legally count as 'adulterated.' Under current law, adulterated meat cannot be sold, so the change would ban these strains from the food supply and give inspectors clear authority to keep contaminated meat off store shelves. The bill was introduced by Senator Kirsten Gillibrand in May 2010 and was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee, where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, especially families with young children and older adults who are most vulnerable to severe E. coli illness, would benefit from tighter controls on contaminated meat. Inspectors would also gain a clear legal standard for acting against meat carrying these bacteria.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds Shiga toxin-producing E. coli to the legal definition of 'adulterated' meat under the Federal Meat Inspection Act, which prohibits selling adulterated meat [S3].
Under the CRS summary, any carcass or meat product contaminated with enterohemorrhagic (EHEC) Shiga toxin-producing serotypes of E. coli would be treated as adulterated [S2].

The Federal Meat Inspection Act already bars adulterated meat from commerce, so the amendment would give USDA inspectors explicit authority to seize or condemn meat carrying these dangerous strains [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Meat producers and processors would bear the cost of stricter standards — more testing, more recalls, and losses when contaminated product is condemned. Those costs could be partly passed to consumers through meat prices.

drawbacks.text: Expanding the adulteration definition would expose meatpackers to more testing costs, product condemnations, and recalls, and some of that cost would likely reach consumers as higher meat prices [S3].
The bill covers only enterohemorrhagic Shiga toxin-producing serotypes, so it would not address other contaminants, and enforcement would still depend on how much testing USDA actually performs [S2].

The bill is a one-line definition change; it contains no new funding, testing requirements, or traceability rules, so its real-world effect would depend entirely on how regulators apply the new standard [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health benefit is real: Shiga toxin-producing E. coli causes serious illness, and giving inspectors explicit authority over contaminated meat is a modest, targeted change. The cost falls on meatpackers in testing and recalls, part of which may be passed to shoppers. As written, the bill is narrow — no new testing programs or funding — so its impact would hinge on regulatory follow-through, but the core tradeoff (safer meat at some cost to producers) is a reasonable one.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee in May 2010, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Senator Kirsten Gillibrand introduced the bill in the Senate on May 27, 2010 [S1].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, and the bill had zero cosponsors [S4].
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, so the bill expired without a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat producers and processors are better off, since the stricter adulteration standard never took effect; consumers did not get the added protection.

for.name: Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Tom Harkin (D-IA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 27, 2010 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and no vote was ever taken, so the partisan shape is unknown.

industries.note: The bill would ban meat carrying dangerous E. coli strains, forcing packers to tighten testing, absorb recalls, and write off contaminated product. Those costs protect consumers from serious foodborne illness but could push meat prices up somewhat.
Retailers would face fewer tainted products reaching their shelves and less recall exposure, but could pay more for supply and pass some cost to shoppers.
